scenes.name: El underground de Londres
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: En Gran Bretaña el LSD circulaba por el mismo tipo de gente que en Estados Unidos: estudiantes de arte, hipsters, bohemios y poetas, muchos llegados desde la CND. Su primera gran reunión fue la International Poetry Incarnation del Albert Hall (junio de 1965: Ginsberg, Trocchi, Burroughs, Adrian Mitchell), filmada por Peter Whitehead. En enero de 1966 John Hopkins y Steve Stollman montaron en el Marquee el primer Spontaneous Underground, intento, como los Acid Tests, de crear un entorno que se acercara a la disrupción perceptiva del LSD; el 13 de marzo, «The Trip», con el grupo de improvisación AMM y el debut en el Marquee de unos Pink Floyd que dejaban las versiones de R&B. En febrero Barry Miles y John Dunbar abrieron la librería Indica (ESP-Disk, Burroughs, Leary, Artaud, Crowley, Gurdjieff, Blavatsky), con la ayuda de Paul McCartney. En abril Miles y Hopkins repartieron en la marcha de la CND THE Global moon-edition Long Hair TIMES.

scenes.name: Arte autodestructivo y happenings
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: La violencia como martillo y no como espejo. Gustav Metzger, cuyas clases en la Ealing Art School inspiraron a Pete Townshend a destrozar guitarras, quería monumentos al poder humano de destruir toda vida, «a Hiroshima». En septiembre de 1966 organizó en Londres el Destruction in Art Symposium con cien artistas de dieciocho países (Ralph Ortiz destrozando un sillón de club, Hermann Nitsch eviscerando corderos, John Latham, Yoko Ono) en un solar bombardeado de Portobello Road; Metzger acabó acusado de exhibición indecente. Allan Kaprow enseñaba en disco a hacer un happening que no se supiera si era arte o vida, y Life dedicaba su portada al «arte LSD». Situaciones, provocaciones, autodestrucción, disturbios: la portada carnicera de los Beatles, la televisión quemada de los Provos y las guitarras rotas de los Who eran provocaciones del mismo orden, una exigencia de que el espectador reaccionara.

scenes.name: El tiempo se fragmenta: retro, camp y McLuhan
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: En otoño de 1966 el impulso lineal del modernismo se había acelerado más allá de lo sostenible y el tiempo se rompía en bucles: el ahora perpetuo o cualquier época sacada a voluntad de unos medios saturados. «Tomorrow Never Knows» y «Tell Me That You Love Me» de James Brown (bucles sobre una grabación en directo, precursora de los breakbeats de la jungle) borraban pasado y futuro en un Ahora eterno. Para McLuhan los jóvenes eran procesadores de datos y había dos niveles de percepción entre quienes nacieron con los medios de masas y quienes no; la televisión convertía el presente en pasado al instante y canibalizaba el pasado. Las series Time Tunnel y Adam Adamant Lives! jugaban con viajes en el tiempo; Beardsley, en el V&A y en la portada de Revolver, sustituyó a lo victoriano; I Was Lord Kitchener’s Valet vendía uniformes antiguos (la casaca de Jagger) y Granny Takes a Trip mezclaba ropa de época y LSD. «Nostalgia del AHORA», había dicho Pauline Boty.

podcast.title: Montreal Bed-In for Peace (1969)
podcast.body: Yoko Ono and John Lennon held their famous "bed-in" in room 1742 at the Fairmont Queen Elizabeth hotel in Montreal in 1969, as a protest against war and a call for peace. "That's where John and Yoko held their famous bed in back in 1969."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Montreal Bed-In for Peace (1969)
podcast.body: Yoko Ono and her partner John Lennon held a week-long non-violent "bed-in for peace" protest in Montreal from May 26 to June 1, 1969, as a novel form of activism against the Vietnam War. This event was a successor to their Amsterdam bed-in and was relocated to Montreal after Lennon was denied entry to the US and a brief, uncomfortable stay in the Bahamas. "On May 26th, June 1st, 1969, he held a bed in for peace protest in Montreal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Notable Visitors During Bed-In (1969)
podcast.body: During their Montreal bed-in, Yoko Ono and John Lennon were visited by prominent figures such as Timothy Leary, Tommy Smothers, Dick Gregory, Murray the K, Al Capp, Alan Ginsburg, and then-Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau. "During the week in Montreal, the couple was visited by Timothy Leary, Tommy Smothers, Dick Gregory, Murray the Kay, Al Cap, Alan Ginsburg, and of course, Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Queen Elizabeth Hotel Stay (1969)
podcast.body: Yoko Ono and John Lennon arrived in Montreal on May 26, 1969, and resided in rooms 1738, 1740, 1742, and 1744 at the Queen Elizabeth Hotel for their bed-in. This location was chosen for its proximity to New York, aiding American press coverage. "John and Yoko flew to Montreal on May 26th and stayed in the room 1738, 1740, 1742, and 1744 at the Queen Elizabeth Hotel."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Role in Nike "Revolution" Deal (1987)
podcast.body: Yoko Ono helped broker the deal for The Beatles' song "Revolution" to be used in a 1987 Nike commercial. Her involvement was driven by the belief that this commercial exposure would introduce her late husband John Lennon's music to a new generation of fans. "She helped broker the deal because she thought it would help bring her late husband's music to a new generation of fans."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Permission for Hotel Suite (1991)
podcast.body: In 1991, Yoko Ono granted permission to the Queen Elizabeth Hotel to begin renting room 1742 in John Lennon's name. Subsequently, the rooms they stayed in were combined and renovated into a large suite, now known as the "John Lennon and Yoko Ono suite." "Years later, in 1991, the Hotel received permission from Yoko Ono to begin renting room 1742 in Lenin's name."

podcast.title: Protecting "Imagine" Lyrics
podcast.body: After John Lennon's death, Yoko Ono repeatedly refused requests to alter the lyrics of "Imagine" to reflect "one religion" instead of "no religion," upholding the song's original intent of a world where no single religion is superior. "Yoko Ono after his death, asked several times if they would permit using that song imagine and changing the song to one religion instead of no religion to which the answer is a resounding no."

xref.title: Bahamas Attempt (1969)
xref.body: Prior to the Montreal bed-in, John Lennon and Yoko Ono intended to host the event in the Bahamas. They flew there on May 24, 1969, but only spent one night because of the oppressive heat, leading them to seek an alternative location in Canada. "They then intended to host the event in the Bahamas, but after flying in on May 24th, 1969, they only spent one night there because of the heat."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Canadian Visa and Hotel Choices (1969)
xref.body: After the Bahamas attempt, John Lennon and Yoko Ono landed in Toronto and were granted a 10-day visitor visa, staying at the King Edward Hotel. They ultimately chose Montreal over Toronto for their bed-in because of its proximity to New York, which would facilitate easier American press coverage. "The choice was between Montreal and Toronto, and ultimately they chose Montreal because it was close to New York, which would make American press coverage much easier."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Hotel Suite Renamed and Renovated (1991, Recently)
xref.body: In 1991, the Queen Elizabeth Hotel received permission from Yoko Ono to begin renting room 1742 in John Lennon's name. More recently, all four rooms (1738, 1740, 1742, and 1744) where the couple stayed were combined into one large suite, featuring two bedrooms, a dining room, two lounges, two bathrooms, a pantry, and virtual reality goggles to experience the view from Lennon's perspective. Today, this renovated suite is known as the "John Lennon and Yoko Ono suite." "Years later, in 1991, the Hotel received permission from Yoko Ono to begin renting room 1742 in Lenin's name."

xref.title: Blood-Infused Vinyl Edition
xref.body: For their 2012 Record Store Day release, "Hetty Fwins," The Flaming Lips created a special clear vinyl edition that visibly contained traces of the band's blood. They also extended this practice to their collaborators, demanding that artists like Chris Martin of Coldplay, Kesha, and Yoko Ono contribute their own blood for ten ultra-rare special editions of the record. "Not only did the clear vinyl vividly show traces of flaming lips blood, but the band also demanded that any of the collaborators on this record also contribute their precious bodily fluid for 10 special editions of the record."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Collaboration with Bowie on "Young Americans"
xref.body: John Lennon collaborated with David Bowie during his "last week in the Strangement" from Yoko Ono, co-writing the lyrics for the song "Fame" in about 20 minutes. He also provided background vocals, notably echoing the word "fame" in the verses of the recording for Bowie's "Young Americans" album. Lennon and Bowie got along famously, and Lennon's assistant, May Pang, later married Bowie's producer, Tony Visconti. "Not only did he and Bowie get along famously but so did Lennon's assistant May Pang and Bowie producer Tony Viscante and they actually ended up getting married."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Collaboration with John Lennon
xref.body: By 1975, Bowie was famous enough that John Lennon was willing to collaborate, co-writing the song "Fame." Lennon, in the middle of his "lost weekend" separation from Yoko Ono, happily partied and worked with Bowie. Their professional and personal relationships extended to their associates, with Lennon's assistant, May Pang, eventually marrying Bowie's producer, Tony Visconti. "By this time Bowie was big enough that someone like John Lennon was willing to hang out and even do a little co-writing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Diverse Musical Career
xref.body: Sean Lennon, the son of John Lennon and Yoko Ono, has had a varied musical career. He has been a member of multiple bands, composed scores for films, produced material for other artists, and released several solo albums. He has also collaborated with prominent figures such as Albert Hammond Jr. of The Strokes, The Flaming Lips, Lady Gaga, and Lana Del Rey. "Sean Lennon is the son of John and Yoko. He's been in a bunch of different bands, scored some films, produced material for other people, recorded a couple of albums on his own, and collaborated on records with people like Albert Hammond Jr. of the Strokes, The Flaming Lips, Lady Gaga, and Lana Del Rey."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence of Arthur Janov's Primal Scream Therapy
xref.body: Roland Orzabal was deeply interested in psychology and psychiatry at the time, particularly fascinated by the teachings of Arthur Janov, the developer of primal scream therapy. This therapeutic approach encourages patients to delve deep into their psyches to uncover the root of their issues, and was also embraced by figures like John Lennon and Yoko Ono. "Roland was deep into psychology and psychiatry at the time. He was particularly fascinated by the teachings of Arthur Janov, the guy behind primal screen therapy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: John Lennon and Yoko Ono - Marital Tensions
xref.body: John Lennon's marriage to Yoko Ono is widely cited as a source of considerable tension and conflict within The Beatles. "John Lennon's marriage to Yoko Ono is said to have caused all kinds of tensions within the Beatles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Marriage to May Pang
xref.body: Tony Visconti, a producer for David Bowie, married May Pang, who was John Lennon's assistant during his "lost weekend" period from Yoko Ono. "Not only did he and Bowie get along famously but so did Lennon's assistant May Pang and Bowie producer Tony Viscante and they actually ended up getting married."
